video_title: How a Third-Party Zero-Day Let Hackers Drain $388 Million From Bitget
gist: Bitget CEO Grace Chen explains the Sept 24 $388M hot/warm wallet hack via a third-party zero-day, the two attack rounds, near-zero freezes ($632K), a $556M protection fund, and ongoing social-engineering attempts. She also fields questions on ThorChain/Near laundering responses and ZachXBT's allegations.

insights.claim: Bitget's $388M hack began on 24 Sept with test withdrawals of 0.48 ETH from the Ethereum hot wallet and 93 TRX from the Tron hot wallet at 18:31 GMT, both below the risk-control threshold, so no alert fired.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Attackers probe below alert thresholds first; threshold-based monitoring is blind to staged probing.

insights.claim: Starting 18:58 GMT the attacker executed 17 large transfers across chains and assets totaling about $361M, and Bitget's reconciliation system flagged the discrepancy 7 minutes after the first large transfer and auto-blocked all user withdrawals.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Detection was fast, yet most of the loss still occurred; detection without containment of the wallet service is insufficient.

insights.claim: The attacker used an undisclosed third-party zero-day in a security product Bitget had adopted to harden security, gained access to a critical internal management system, impersonated users to create fraudulent withdrawal orders, and injected them directly into the wallet service, which executed them.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Security vendors themselves are a supply-chain attack surface; the compromise was at the hot/warm wallet orchestration layer, not a cold-wallet signing flow.

insights.claim: After the transfers the attackers deleted traces of the fraudulent withdrawal orders, forcing investigators to examine a wider set of systems to find the root cause.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Log tampering lengthens incident response and delays containment.

insights.claim: A second round of roughly $30M was stolen between 20:55 and 21:23 because Bitget consolidated hot and warm wallet funds into cold wallets, re-enabling wallet transfers while it could not rule out private key compromise; the last malicious transaction was at 21:23, under three hours after the first.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Emergency fund sweeps can reopen the attack window if the compromise is not yet scoped, a trade-off incident responders face.

insights.claim: Bitget says its hack differs from Bybit's: Bybit's was a clear single cause (Safe wallet interface affecting a cold wallet), whereas Bitget's involved hot and warm wallets, multiple systems and multiple blockchains, making root-cause analysis harder.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Hot-wallet operational compromises are more diffuse and slower to diagnose than cold-wallet UI attacks.

insights.claim: Bitget declined to name the vendor or vulnerability, said it accepts full responsibility rather than blaming the third party, and promised an incident report within about a week while having notified the vendor of the flaw.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Watch the incident report for vendor identity; other exchanges using the same product could be exposed to the same zero-day.

insights.claim: Only about $632K of the $388M stolen was frozen as of the interview, with Tether and Circle named as main freezers, which implies near-total laundering success so far.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Recovery odds are very low (about 0.16%), consistent with prior large hacks.

insights.claim: Bitget published a dashboard tracking all stolen-fund addresses, offered a 5% bounty for voluntarily freezing and another 5% for returning funds, and will pay it even to parties that already froze funds or donate it if they decline, explicitly copying the Bybit playbook.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: The 5%+5% bounty template is becoming the industry standard response to major exchange hacks.

insights.claim: Circle acted quickly on Bitget's case, and Laura Shin noted this contrasted with Drift's roughly $280M incident where, per her earlier episode, it did not act; Bitget's Grace Chen attributed it possibly to rule changes or to the fast publication of all information.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin
insights.so_what: Stablecoin issuer freeze behavior may depend on how quickly and transparently victims publish addresses.

insights.claim: Bitget asked ThorChain to refuse service to hack-linked addresses; ThorChain publicly declined, and rival exchanges accused it of inconsistency because it halted its system when it was itself the victim. Grace Chen said she does not want ThorChain to abandon open source and had not had a direct conversation with its developers.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Permissionless cross-chain swap venues remain the main laundering rails and a governance fault line.

insights.claim: Near Intents built an intelligent shield layer that detects anomalies in data flows and aggregates signals from KYT providers and independent researchers to decide whether a transaction proceeds, while the deployment stays open source; Grace Chen praised this as the ideal compromise and its stance that permissionless does not mean neutral.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Compliance layers on top of open-source protocols could become a competitive differentiator and a template regulators favor.

insights.claim: Bitget argued that easy laundering of stolen funds directly increases the number and size of hacks, since attackers face few obstacles cashing out.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Making laundering harder is a deterrence lever; expect pressure on swap protocols and privacy-adjacent venues.

insights.claim: Grace Chen said North Korean laundering typically splits funds into very small chunks (down to about $10,000), uses tiny exchanges such as FixedFloat, and routes through privacy coins like Zcash and Monero; large exchanges like Bitget are not their first choice because of KYC/KYT.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Small instant-swap services and privacy coins are the likely exit points to watch on-chain.

insights.claim: Bitget floated an industry coalition of the largest exchanges, security firms, intelligence agencies and regulators to prevent laundering of stolen funds.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: A formal coalition would be a new industry structure; so far it is only an idea.

themes.theme: Balance sheet, protection fund and user flows

insights.claim: Bitget's Protection Fund, created in mid-2022 after the bear-market exchange failures and held in open, on-chain wallets, was used at scale for the first time; it now holds about $556M mostly in BTC and Bitget promised to restore it above $300M (initial target $200M, later raised to $300M) within a week using company capital.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: A transparent, self-insurance fund over 1.4x the loss let the exchange absorb the $388M hit without socializing losses; this is a credibility template for exchanges.

insights.claim: Bitget saw lower-than-expected withdrawals after reopening: ETH withdrawals started 08:00 UTC and one hour in, ETH inflow to Bitget was 9,674 ETH versus roughly 9,023 ETH outflow, a net inflow; BTC withdrawals began the day before.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: No bank-run dynamic after a nine-figure hack suggests user trust anchored by the protection fund.

insights.claim: Grace Chen said the hack did not change Bitget's main financial plans, including a possible IPO in about three years, and that the company has stayed in contact with law enforcement and regulators.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Management signals the IPO path is intact; regulatory reaction remains the uncertainty.

insights.claim: Grace Chen said three exchanges closed or went bankrupt or withdrew in June and July of this year, which she compared to the stress that motivated Bitget's 2022 protection fund.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Smaller-exchange attrition is ongoing; scale and reserves are consolidating share to larger venues.

insights.claim: Grace Chen said the day after the hack, attackers impersonated a major investment firm's team with several actors playing roles and nearly started a real conversation with her before she verified through another known channel with the firm's founder and found it was a scam.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Hackers exploit post-incident chaos when victims seek help from many outside partners; out-of-band identity verification is essential.

insights.claim: Grace Chen said the pattern behind many North Korean attacks begins as social engineering aimed at public figures, who are known to give many interviews and talk to many outside partners, with attackers impersonating those contacts; a request to use an unfamiliar livestream tool instead of Zoom or Google Meet is a red flag.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Executives and media-facing founders are primary targets; unusual meeting platforms are a practical tell.

insights.claim: Bitget's post-incident measures: isolate and take offline all related servers and systems to preserve forensic evidence, revoke and reissue all internal credentials, and require multi-party approvals for critical operations on highly sensitive systems.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Standard containment checklist; also an implicit admission those approvals were not sufficiently multi-party before.

insights.claim: Grace Chen conceded Bitget did not do enough due diligence on third-party vendors and will change that, and that there is a tension between sharing details with partners and customers and revealing its security architecture, team and vendors to attackers.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Vendor risk management is the lesson; incident reports may be deliberately limited in detail.

insights.claim: Grace Chen said Bitget could not say whether the post-hack social engineering was North Korea or opportunistic scammers, saying it could be both.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Attribution to North Korea for the main hack is not confirmed in this conversation beyond Laura Shin's framing of hallmarks.

insights.claim: Laura Shin recounted that ZachXBT earlier alleged price-manipulation schemes originated on Bitget and Gate, claimed 95% of the Lab token supply was held by insiders and that insiders withdrew about $500M from Bitget, and later tweeted five pseudonyms of Chinese OTC launderers moving North Korean funds from this hack.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin
insights.so_what: On-chain sleuths are shifting from hostile to helpful on this case; reputational overhang on Bitget remains.

insights.claim: Grace Chen did not directly respond to the manipulation allegations, saying the tokens are listed on many exchanges (Binance, Gate, Bybit, OKX and others), so manipulation cannot be attributed to Bitget alone, and said Bitget had not paid ZachXBT or talked to him directly.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Defense is multi-venue listing, not a rebuttal of the specific claims; the allegations are unresolved.

insights.claim: Bitget works formally with SlowMist and Mandiant on incident reports and informally with volunteer white-hat groups such as Seal 911, and credits their independent tracing.
insights.speaker: Grace Chen (Bitget CEO)
insights.so_what: Bitget outsourced forensics to named firms, so the incident report will carry third-party credibility.
